title: Firewalls
desc: What firewalls do, NGFW, UTM, VPN and SD-WAN

pages.t: A firewall watches the traffic going in and out of a network and decides what is allowed. It usually sits between a trusted network (the office) and an untrusted one (the internet). Think of a guard checking every visitor against a list.
g: A security device or software that allows or blocks network traffic by rules.

pages.t: Each rule says what to do with traffic matching a source, destination, port, protocol or application: allow, deny or inspect more. The first firewalls simply checked addresses and ports in each packet.
g: A small chunk of data travelling over a network.
A numbered door for a service, like 443 for secure web.

pages.t: Firewalls can be network-based (a box at the edge) or host-based (software on a PC). Customers of every size usually want one at the internet connection.
g: Firewall software running on one computer.

quiz.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Allows or blocks traffic by rules
quiz.w: It monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on security rules.

quiz.q: Where is a network firewall normally placed?
quiz.w: It sits between, for example, the office LAN and the internet.

quiz.q: Which is a host-based firewall?
o: A box at the office edge
quiz.w: Host-based firewalls run on the computer they protect.

pages.t: Firewalls group networks into zones with different trust levels: LAN (inside), WAN (outside, the internet), sometimes Wi-Fi and DMZ. Rules then say which zone may talk to which.
g: A group of network segments treated with the same trust level.
The outside, usually the internet side.

pages.t: A common default: traffic from LAN to WAN is allowed, but traffic from WAN to LAN is dropped. Staff can browse out, strangers cannot walk in. Extra rules open specific, deliberate exceptions.
A DMZ is a middle zone for services that the outside needs to reach, like a web or mail server. If one of them is hacked, the damage is kept away from the internal network.
g: Demilitarized zone: a buffer network for public-facing servers.

quiz.q: What is the typical default between zones?
o: WAN to LAN allowed, LAN to WAN dropped
LAN to WAN allowed, WAN to LAN dropped
quiz.w: Inside users can go out; unsolicited traffic from outside is dropped.

quiz.q: A customer hosts a public web server. Where should it go?
o: Directly on the WAN with no firewall
quiz.w: A DMZ exposes the needed services while shielding the internal network.

quiz.q: What is the point of zones?
o: Different trust levels with rules between them
quiz.w: Zones let the firewall apply rules based on trust between areas.

pages.t: A stateful firewall tracks each connection from start to finish and uses context from earlier packets. It knows a reply belongs to a request that went out. It decides on address, port and protocol.
g: Tracking whole connections instead of judging each packet alone.

pages.t: A next-generation firewall adds application awareness, intrusion prevention, web filtering by reputation and threat intelligence. It can see that traffic on port 443 is a video call or a file-sharing app, not just "web".
g: Next-Generation Firewall: a firewall that understands applications and users and adds threat protection.

pages.t: NGFW rules can target users and groups by linking to a directory service, plus inspect encrypted (TLS) traffic. So the rule can say: marketing may use this app, guests may not. That is easier to manage than IP lists.
g: Opening encrypted traffic to check it for threats.
A central list of users, such as Active Directory.

quiz.q: What does a stateful firewall track?
o: Whole connections from start to end
quiz.w: It uses context from earlier packets in the same connection.

quiz.q: Which feature separates an NGFW from a simple stateful firewall?
quiz.w: NGFWs go beyond stateful inspection with app awareness, IPS and more.
g: Intrusion Prevention System, which blocks detected attacks.

quiz.q: A customer wants marketing to use a social app while others cannot. What do you point to?
quiz.w: Next-gen rules can target applications and user groups.

pages.h: UTM: many tools in one box
pages.t: UTM bundles firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, VPN and web filtering into a single device with one console. That means fewer boxes and one place to manage them, which often suits teams with little IT staff.
g: Unified Threat Management: several security functions in one device.
Blocking access to chosen websites or categories.

pages.t: IDS only detects and reports. IPS sits in the traffic path and can block attacks. Signature-based checks catch known attacks; anomaly-based ones flag unusual behaviour but can raise false alarms.

A sandbox runs suspicious files in a safe, isolated space to watch what they do before they reach users. It helps with new threats that no signature knows yet. These features are often licensed as subscriptions.
g: Testing suspicious files in an isolated environment.

quiz.q: What is the difference between IDS and IPS?
o: IDS can block, IPS only reports
IPS can block, IDS only reports
quiz.w: An IPS sits in line and actively blocks detected intrusions.

quiz.q: What does a sandbox do?
o: Runs suspicious files in isolation to see what they do
quiz.w: Sandboxing catches novel threats by observing behaviour in a safe space.

quiz.q: A small firm has one IT person and wants one box and one console. What fits?
quiz.w: UTM combines functions in one device with one console, which usually suits small teams.

pages.t: A VPN wraps traffic in an encrypted tunnel across a public network like the internet. The traffic stays private, as if both ends were on the same LAN. Firewalls very often include VPN functions.
g: Virtual Private Network: an encrypted tunnel over the internet.
A protected path through a network.

pages.t: Site-to-site VPNs link whole networks: two gateways create the tunnel, and everyone at both sites reaches the other side. Typical case: a branch office connecting to head office or a data centre.
g: The device at the edge of a site that makes the tunnel.

pages.t: Remote access VPNs let individual users connect to the company network from home or on the road. Each laptop opens its own tunnel, usually through client software. That is the home office case.
g: Software on the user's own device.

quiz.q: A company wants its branch to reach head office files. Which VPN?
quiz.w: Site-to-site links whole networks through gateways at each location.

quiz.q: An employee works from home and needs the file server. Which VPN?
quiz.w: Remote access gives individual devices their own tunnel into the network.

quiz.q: What does a VPN tunnel do?
o: Encrypts traffic over a public network
quiz.w: It protects traffic crossing the internet by encrypting it.

pages.t: IPsec is an IETF standards-based suite that encrypts IP packets. Tunnels are set up using IKE. It is the classic choice for site-to-site links, and the newer IKEv2 copes well when a phone changes network.
g: A standard way to encrypt and wrap IP traffic.
The protocol that sets up the IPsec tunnel.

pages.t: SSL/TLS VPNs run over the same protocol as secure websites. Because it looks like ordinary web traffic, it tends to get through networks that only allow web traffic. Many remote-access setups use them.
g: The encryption used by HTTPS websites.

pages.t: Both are secure when set up well. Rule of thumb: IPsec for linking sites, SSL where users sit behind restrictive hotel or guest networks. Always ask which the firewalls at both ends support.

quiz.q: Why does an SSL VPN often work on strict guest networks?
o: It uses the same protocol as HTTPS
quiz.w: Because it looks like normal web traffic, it passes where web is allowed.

quiz.q: Which is the classic standards-based suite for site-to-site tunnels?
quiz.w: IPsec is an IETF suite that encrypts IP packets.

quiz.q: What should you check when linking two sites with VPN?
o: That both firewalls support the chosen VPN type
quiz.w: Both ends must speak the same VPN method.

pages.t: SD-WAN manages a WAN with software. It builds encrypted tunnels between sites, often over ordinary internet lines, and steers each application over the best available link.
g: Software-Defined WAN: software that manages and optimises links between sites.

pages.t: A site can use fibre, broadband and 4G/5G together. SD-WAN spots outages and fails over to a working link. Important apps like voice get priority. The caveat: the internet gives no guaranteed performance.
g: Automatic switch to a backup link when the main one fails.

pages.t: Settings are pushed from one central place, cloud or on-site, to every branch. Chains with many shops or offices like this, and some firewalls include SD-WAN features. Not every small customer needs it.

quiz.q: What does SD-WAN do?
o: Manages several links between sites and picks the best path per application
quiz.w: It uses software to steer traffic over the best link and fail over on outages.

quiz.q: A retail chain has 40 shops, each with fibre and a 4G backup. Which concept fits?
quiz.w: Many sites with several links managed centrally is the SD-WAN use case.

quiz.q: What is a caveat of SD-WAN over internet links?
o: There are no guaranteed performance levels
quiz.w: Internet traffic has no end-to-end performance guarantee like carrier private lines.

pages.t: Hardware appliances are the usual box at the office. Virtual firewalls run on hypervisors on-site or in public clouds. Cloud-native ones are built to secure cloud workloads at scale. Pick by where the protected systems live.
g: Software that runs virtual machines, such as VMware or Hyper-V.

pages.t: Firewalls can be managed on-premises (a console or the box itself) or from a cloud portal, which some vendors offer. Cloud management helps resellers handle many small customers from one view.
g: Hosted and run at the customer's own site.

pages.t: Size by the number of users, the internet speed, and which protections will be switched on, since inspection features slow throughput. Ask for growth plans too. Check the maker's datasheet instead of guessing.
g: How much traffic a device can process per second.

quiz.q: Where would a virtual firewall fit best?
o: Protecting workloads in a private or public cloud
quiz.w: Virtual firewalls run on hypervisors or in public clouds.

quiz.q: A reseller supports 50 small customers. What management style helps most?
o: Visiting each site with a laptop
quiz.w: Cloud management lets one view cover many small sites.

quiz.q: Which affects firewall sizing?
o: Users, internet speed and enabled protections
quiz.w: Inspection features reduce throughput, so enabled protections matter.

pages.t: Small offices want simple, bundled protection and easy management. Mid-size firms add VPNs, user rules and several sites. Large or regulated customers need depth, logs and certifications. Match the box to the customer's skill and risk.
g: Official proof a product meets a security standard.

pages.t: How many users and sites? Remote workers? Who manages IT? Any public servers? Compliance needs? Current firewall and when its licence or support runs out? Renewal dates are good conversation starters.
g: A subscription that unlocks security features and updates.

pages.t: Think in categories, not brands: UTM-style all-in-ones for small business, enterprise NGFW platforms, cloud-managed small-site boxes, and plain consumer routers. The honest sales point is fit, support and local service.

quiz.q: Which customer most needs an all-in-one, simple-to-manage box?
o: A 10-person office with no IT staff
quiz.w: UTM-style bundles suit small teams with limited IT resources.

quiz.q: Which is a good opening question?
o: When does your current firewall licence expire?
quiz.w: Licence and support expiry reveal timing and the customer's current setup.

quiz.q: Which is a competitor category and not a brand?
quiz.w: Categories like consumer routers help compare without pushing brands.
